Neuroscience · Batch 44 · Lecture Series

The Brainstem

A level-by-level journey through the medulla oblongata, pons, and midbrain — cranial nerve nuclei, long tracts, the reticular formation, and the clinical reasoning built on top of them.

Lecture by Dr. Hassan Salaheldeen · Compiled by H. Salaheldeen & Orca

Learning Objectives

  1. Identify the brainstem nuclei associated with the cranial nerves and locate them on a brainstem cross-section.
  2. Identify the cranial nerves at the point where they connect to (attach to) the brainstem.
  3. Describe the reticular formation — its connections, functions, and structure.

Introduction

  • The brainstem is composed of three parts: the medulla oblongata, the pons, and the midbrain.
  • It extends from the pyramidal decussation inferiorly to the posterior commissure superiorly.
  • Its blood supply comes from the vertebrobasilar system (vertebral arteries → basilar artery and their branches).
  • It gives rise to cranial nerves III through XII (the first two cranial nerves, olfactory and optic, do not arise from the brainstem).
High-yield — Brainstem extent: pyramidal decussation (inferior limit) → posterior commissure (superior limit).

Surface Anatomy of the Brainstem

Anterior (Ventral) Surface

Working from below upward

  • The pyramids sit anteriorly — shaped like an inverted pyramid, broad base below and narrow apex above. Lateral to each pyramid is the olive (an oval elevation overlying the inferior olivary nucleus).
  • CN XII (hypoglossal) emerges in the groove between the pyramid and the olive.
  • Behind the olive, three nerve rootlets emerge in sequence: CN IX (glossopharyngeal), CN X (vagus), and CN XI (accessory) — "nine, ten, eleven."
  • At the junction between the pons and medulla, in the midline, CN VI (abducens) exits.
  • Laterally, this pons–medulla junction is known clinically as the cerebellopontine angle (CPA) — the angle between the cerebellum and the pons. CN VII (facial) and CN VIII (vestibulocochlear) emerge here, making the CPA a key site for pathology such as vestibular schwannoma.
  • Within the pons itself, laterally, CN V (trigeminal) emerges.
  • At the pontomesencephalic junction (midbrain–pons junction), in the midline, CN III (oculomotor) exits anteriorly.
  • CN IV (trochlear) is unique: it is the only cranial nerve that exits from the posterior (dorsal) aspect of the brainstem, then curves around to reach the front.
  • Superior to the midbrain lie the optic chiasm and optic nerves; moving posteriorly from the chiasm gives the optic tract.
High-yield — CN IV: the only cranial nerve to exit from the dorsal brainstem surface.

Posterior (Dorsal) Surface

  • The midbrain shows four protruding elevations called the colliculi: two superior colliculi above and two inferior colliculi below.
  • These four colliculi together form the tectum — the posterior third of the midbrain (the midbrain is divided into basis, tegmentum, and tectum).
  • Etymology tip: tectum literally means "cover" or "roof." If the body is imagined in a bent, quadrupedal (animal) posture — ventral structures pointing inferiorly and dorsal structures pointing superiorly — the tectum sits like a roof over the brainstem, and the tegmentum ("covering") lies beneath it, with the basis furthest anterior/inferior.
  • Below the colliculi is the fourth ventricle, tent-shaped. If the fourth ventricle is a tilted tent, its floor is the brainstem and its roof is the cerebellum.
  • The cerebellar peduncles connect the cerebellum to each part of the brainstem — though there is overlap between them: superior cerebellar peduncle (midbrain–cerebellum), middle cerebellar peduncle (pons–cerebellum), inferior cerebellar peduncle (medulla–cerebellum).
  • With the cerebellum removed, the lateral recess between the pons and the medulla — where CN VII and CN VIII would run beneath the cerebellum — is the cerebellopontine angle (CPA).
  • The area postrema lies at the caudal end of the fourth ventricle floor — this is the vomiting (chemoreceptor trigger) zone. Any irritation here can trigger vomiting.
  • The tuberculum gracilis and tuberculum cuneatus are visible swellings that overlie the nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus respectively.
    • Gracilis carries information from the lower limb (lumbosacral levels).
    • Cuneatus carries information from the upper limb (cervicothoracic levels).
Clinical — Area postrema: a key structure behind projectile vomiting, especially the vomiting associated with raised intracranial pressure (ICP). Classic ICP-related vomiting and headache are worst in the early morning, upon waking.

Medulla Oblongata

CaudalMidRostral
LEVEL · Caudal Medulla

Cross-Section Through the Caudal Medulla

This level resembles the spinal cord more than any other brainstem level — it is the transition zone where spinal tracts continue upward and the first purely medullary structures appear.

  1. Pyramid — anterior; carries corticospinal (and corticonuclear) fibers descending from the cortex.
  2. Nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus — posterior; give rise to internal arcuate fibers that cross the midline (decussate) to form the medial lemniscus.
  3. Anterior and posterior spinocerebellar tracts — carry unconscious proprioceptive information toward the cerebellum.
  4. Inferior olivary nucleus — postero-lateral to the pyramid; a large, convoluted (folded) nucleus visible as the surface "olive."
  5. Accessory cuneate nucleus — sits beside the nucleus cuneatus; gives rise to the cuneocerebellar tract, the upper-limb equivalent of the posterior spinocerebellar tract (it is "accessory" because it was added alongside the already-named cuneatus/cuneocerebellar system).

Additional structures at this level include the central canal, the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) just posterior to the midline (where motor cranial nerve nuclei intermix signals from both sides), the nucleus ambiguus surrounded by reticular formation, the spinothalamic tract (medial to the spinocerebellar tracts), and, lateral to the central canal, the spinal tract and spinal nucleus of CN V (trigeminal).

High-yield: gracilis/cuneatus → internal arcuate fibers → decussate → medial lemniscus.
Clinical vignette — the trigeminal spinal nucleus and tract extend to C1–C2: A patient in their 40s–50s presented with facial numbness and limb weakness. Because the two most important questions in any CNS presentation are "What is the lesion, and where is the lesion?," and because signs of raised ICP (headache, vomiting, visual disturbance) were absent, the localisation pointed to the high cervical cord — where the trigeminal spinal nucleus and tract still run. Imaging confirmed a schwannoma at C1, which produced both facial sensory loss and limb weakness simultaneously. Careful localisation before ordering costly imaging (such as MRI) is emphasized as core clinical practice.
Clinical — Trigeminal neuralgia: inflammation/compression of CN V is considered one of the most severe pain syndromes a person can experience. The three divisions cover distinct territories: ophthalmic (forehead to eye), maxillary (eye to angle of mouth), and mandibular (angle of mouth to jaw). Patients may report pain and/or numbness (paraesthesia).
LEVEL · Mid-Medulla

Cross-Section Through the Mid-Medulla

The reticular formation becomes more prominent at this level, and the fourth ventricle becomes clearer. The nucleus gracilis and cuneatus (seen at the caudal level) have already given rise to their tracts and are no longer visible; new structures appear:

  1. Hypoglossal nucleus (CN XII) — posterior, near the midline.
  2. Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (CN X) — antero-lateral to the hypoglossal nucleus; contains preganglionic parasympathetic cell bodies whose fibers travel in CN X.
  3. Solitary nucleus — the special sense (taste) nucleus, receiving fibers from CN VII, IX, and X. ("Solitarius" = solitary/singular — a distinctive nucleus with a unique, dedicated visceral/taste role; it also contributes to the vomiting reflex, cardiovascular regulation via baroreceptor input, and respiratory control.)
  4. Medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) — "yolks together" (interconnects) the motor cranial nerve nuclei of the two sides so that signals are coordinated across the midline.
  5. Tectospinal tract — descending fibers running from the midbrain colliculi to lower motor neurons of the cervical spinal cord (mediates reflex head/neck turning toward visual/auditory stimuli).
  6. Nucleus ambiguus — a lower motor neuron nucleus sending fibers into CN IX and CN X (motor supply to pharynx/larynx).
  7. Medial lemniscus — formed from the decussated arcuate fibers of gracilis/cuneatus; carries fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception.
  8. Inferior cerebellar peduncle — becoming visible laterally.

The inferior vestibular nucleus (CN VIII) and the spinal nucleus/tract of CN V are also present at this level, alongside the lateral spinothalamic tract, still ascending toward the thalamus.

High-yield — Solitary nucleus: the shared taste (special visceral afferent) relay for CN VII, IX, and X.
High-yield — Nucleus ambiguus: motor nucleus for CN IX and X (pharynx/larynx).
LEVEL · Rostral Medulla

Cross-Section Through the Rostral Medulla

  1. Spinothalamic tracts (spinal lemniscus) — ascending, still en route to the thalamus; carry pain and temperature (the lateral spinothalamic division specifically).
  2. Spinal nucleus and tract of CN V — continues at this level; the tract descends from the pons down to C1–C2, explaining how a high cervical lesion can mimic a trigeminal lesion.
  3. Inferior cerebellar peduncle — now contains three tracts: olivocerebellar, cuneocerebellar, and posterior spinocerebellar fibers.

Also visible: the hypoglossal nucleus, the solitary nucleus and tract (CN VII, IX, X), the MLF, the medial lemniscus, the inferior olivary nucleus, the pyramids, and — new at this level — the cochlear nuclei, the auditory (hearing) division of CN VIII (the vestibular division handles balance).

Memory aid for the spinocerebellar pathways: rename "posterior" spinocerebellar as dorsal spinocerebellar — "DD" = Dorsal, Direct (uncrossed, two-neuron pathway), entering the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle. The anterior spinocerebellar tract, by contrast, crosses (decussates twice, net effect largely uncrossed) and enters via the superior cerebellar peduncle.
High-yield: Lissauer's tract is where first-order pain/temperature fibers enter the spinal cord before ascending as the spinothalamic tract.

Pons

CaudalMidRostral
LEVEL · Caudal Pons

Cross-Section Through the Caudal Pons

The fourth ventricle is now wide open posteriorly (its "roof" is formed by the cerebellum). Cranial nerves V through VIII arise in the pons.

  1. Medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) — anterior to the fourth ventricle, in the midline.
  2. Abducens nucleus (CN VI) — lies lateral to the MLF, in the midline of the floor; it lies directly under the facial colliculus.
  3. Internal genu of CN VII — the facial nerve's motor fibers loop ("genu" = knee/bend) around the abducens nucleus before exiting laterally at the CPA; this loop produces the surface elevation called the facial colliculus.
  4. Medial lemniscus — anterior, in the midline.
  5. Corticospinal and corticonuclear tracts — run in the base (basis) of the pons, anteriorly — these continue down to become the medullary pyramids.
  6. Facial motor nucleus (CN VII) — lateral, gives rise to the fibers that form the internal genu.

Continuing:

  1. Spinal nucleus and tract of CN V — lateral, continuing down from the pons.
  2. Spinothalamic tracts (spinal lemniscus) — lateral.
  3. Vestibular nuclei (CN VIII) — present here as well, reflecting overlap between adjacent levels (like the cerebellar peduncles, several structures span more than one level).
  4. Inferior and middle cerebellar peduncle — lateral.
  5. Central tegmental tract — a fiber pathway traversing (running through) the reticular formation, located centrally between the medial lemniscus and the MLF.
High-yield — Facial colliculus: formed by the internal genu of CN VII looping around the CN VI (abducens) nucleus.
LEVEL · Mid-Pons

Cross-Section Through the Mid-Pons

The fourth ventricle is beginning to narrow at this level. The same three fibre columns keep their front-to-back order: medial lemniscus (most anterior) → central tegmental tract (middle) → MLF (most posterior).

  1. Raphe nuclei — midline; serotonergic; functionally linked to the MLF region and to pain modulation.
  2. Deep pontine nuclei and transverse pontine fibers — anteriorly, within the basis pontis; these relay cortical input to the contralateral cerebellum via the middle cerebellar peduncle.
  3. Superior cerebellar peduncle — the main outflow pathway of the cerebellum; also carries decussating anterior spinocerebellar fibers.

The middle cerebellar peduncle is visible as well (it belongs primarily to the pons — connecting pontine nuclei to the cerebellum), and the corticospinal tract remains visible anteriorly.

LEVEL · Rostral Pons

Cross-Section Through the Rostral Pons

  1. Mesencephalic nucleus (of CN V) — mediates unconscious proprioception for the head: the automatic, non-conscious adjustment of head/jaw position (e.g., correcting head posture reflexively) without deliberate thought.
  2. Locus coeruleus — a pigmented (blue-grey) nucleus and the primary source of norepinephrine for the brain.
  3. Cerebral aqueduct — connects the third and fourth ventricles.
  4. Periaqueductal gray — surrounds the aqueduct; involved in pain modulation and is a source of serotonin.
High-yield — Locus coeruleus: main norepinephrine source in the CNS. Periaqueductal gray: pain modulation, serotonergic.

Midbrain

CaudalRostral
LEVEL · Caudal Midbrain

Cross-Section Through the Caudal Midbrain

The midbrain has three regions: a posterior tectum, an intermediate tegmentum, and an anterior basis. The cerebral aqueduct lies between the tectum and the tegmentum. At the caudal level, the tectum consists of the inferior colliculi.

  1. Medial lemniscus — now positioned anteriorly, having rotated forward through the levels.
  2. Inferior colliculus — the auditory relay nucleus of the tectum at this level.
  3. Trochlear nucleus (CN IV) — a lower motor neuron nucleus that innervates the superior oblique muscle; located at the level of the inferior colliculus.
  4. Crus cerebri (also called basis pedunculi cerebri or cerebral peduncle) — composed of descending corticospinal, corticonuclear, and corticopontine fibers; paired ventral columns that, together with the adjacent substantia nigra, give a "Mickey Mouse ears" appearance in cross-section.
High-yield: the trochlear nucleus sits at the level of the inferior colliculus.
LEVEL · Rostral Midbrain

Cross-Section Through the Rostral Midbrain

  1. Superior colliculus — the visual relay nucleus of the tectum at this level.
  2. Oculomotor nucleus (CN III) — a lower motor neuron nucleus that innervates the majority of the extraocular muscles. Of the six extraocular muscles, CN III supplies four (superior, inferior, and medial rectus, plus inferior oblique) and levator palpebrae superioris, plus parasympathetic fibers to the pupil.
  3. Red nucleus — part of the primitive (extrapyramidal) motor system, involved in movement coordination.
  4. Ventral tegmental area — source of dopamine; involved in the brain's reward system.
  5. Spinothalamic and trigeminothalamic tracts — mixing together as they ascend toward the thalamus.
  6. Medial lemniscus — anterior, as at the caudal level.

Of the four extraocular muscles not supplied by CN III, the superior oblique is supplied by CN IV (trochlear) and the lateral rectus by CN VI (abducens).

High-yield: the oculomotor nucleus sits at the level of the superior colliculus (trochlear = inferior colliculus level).
Clinical — CN VI vulnerability: the abducens nerve has the longest intracranial course of any cranial nerve, making it the most frequently injured — including as a false localizing sign in raised ICP. A CN VI palsy paralyses the lateral rectus, so the affected eye is unopposed by the medial rectus and deviates medially (nasally) — i.e., the eye "turns in."

The Reticular Formation

Connections, Function, and Structure

The reticular formation (RF) is a diffuse network of interconnected neurons that runs through the core (tegmentum) of the brainstem, from the medulla through the pons to the midbrain. It is not a single discrete nucleus but a distributed system, best appreciated across the levels already covered:

  • Structure: in the caudal and mid-medulla, the reticular formation surrounds the nucleus ambiguus. In the midbrain, the entire tegmentum is considered reticular formation territory.
  • Connections: the central tegmental tract is a key fiber pathway that traverses (runs through) the reticular formation, linking it across pontine levels; the tract sits centrally, between the medial lemniscus (anterior) and the MLF (posterior).
  • Functions distributed across its components include:
    • Cardiovascular and respiratory regulation (via medullary "centers," closely tied to the solitary nucleus and area postrema).
    • The vomiting reflex (area postrema / solitary nucleus).
    • Pain modulation and serotonin production (periaqueductal gray, raphe nuclei).
    • Norepinephrine output to the whole brain (locus coeruleus).
    • Level of consciousness / arousal (ascending reticular activating system).
High-yield: the respiratory and cardiac centers are located in the reticular formation of the medulla oblongata.

Corticonuclear (Corticobulbar) Fibers

The General Rule — and Its One Exception

  • Corticonuclear fibers project bilaterally to all motor cranial nerve nuclei, except the facial nucleus.
  • The division of the facial nucleus that supplies the upper face (frontalis, orbicularis oculi, and above) receives bilateral corticonuclear input.
  • The division that supplies the lower face receives only contralateral corticonuclear input.

Custom schematic — forehead-sparing rule for localising facial nerve palsy.

Clinical bottom line: a stroke affecting the internal capsule (UMN lesion) causes contralateral lower-face weakness with a spared forehead. Bell's palsy and other LMN lesions of CN VII cause ipsilateral weakness of the entire half of the face, including the forehead.

Cranial Nerve Attachment & Nuclei — Full Summary

The "2–4–4" Exit Rule

Cranial nerves attach to the brainstem in a 2–4–4 pattern, from rostral to caudal:

Mnemonic: like a football/soccer line-up — 2 forward (midbrain), 4 midfield (pons), 4 defence (medulla).

Mnemonics & Memory Aids

2 - 4 - 4
Midbrain gives 2 (III, IV); pons gives 4 (V–VIII); medulla gives 4 (IX–XII). Like a team formation: 2 forward, 4 midfield, 4 defence.
DD
Dorsal spinocerebellar tract = Dorsal + Direct (uncrossed); enters via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Mickey Mouse Ears
The crus cerebri (paired, flanking the substantia nigra) give the ventral midbrain its "Mickey Mouse" silhouette; they carry the corticospinal tract.
Roof · Blanket · Floor
Tectum = roof/cover (posterior); tegmentum = covering (middle); basis = base (anterior) — think of the brainstem bent into an animal/quadrupedal posture.
Nine, Ten, Eleven
CN IX, X, XI exit in sequence just behind the olive, in the post-olivary sulcus.
Etymology Tip
Whenever a new anatomical term appears, look up its root/etymology — it locks the meaning in far better than rote memorisation (e.g., tectum = "cover/roof").

Clinical Pearls

  • Localisation first: "What is the lesion? Where is the lesion?" — the two most important questions in clinical neurology. Careful bedside localisation can spare a patient an unnecessary, costly MRI.
  • Raised ICP: suspect it when a patient reports projectile vomiting and a severe headache that are both worst immediately on waking in the early morning (linked to the area postrema).
  • Medical student syndrome: a routine morning headache does not, by itself, mean raised ICP — avoid over-interpreting common symptoms while learning.
  • High cervical lesions can mimic trigeminal disease: because the spinal tract/nucleus of CN V extends to C1–C2, a lesion there (e.g., schwannoma) can cause facial numbness together with limb weakness.
  • Trigeminal neuralgia is considered one of the most severe pain syndromes; know the three sensory divisions (ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular).
  • CN VI palsy: longest intracranial nerve course → most vulnerable to stretch/compression, including as a false localising sign of raised ICP; causes medial deviation of the eye (unopposed medial rectus).
  • Facial nerve lesion localisation: forehead spared = UMN (central) lesion; forehead involved = LMN lesion (e.g., Bell's palsy), because only the lower-face division of the facial nucleus lacks bilateral cortical input.
  • Cerebellopontine angle (CPA): the classic site for a vestibular schwannoma, presenting with combined CN VII and VIII deficits (facial weakness, hearing loss, imbalance).

Glossary — Difficult Vocabulary & Etymology

Decussation
The crossing of a fiber tract from one side of the CNS to the other (e.g., pyramidal decussation, decussation of the medial lemniscus).
Colliculus
Latin "small hill" — the four dorsal midbrain elevations (2 superior, visual; 2 inferior, auditory).
Tectum
Latin "roof/cover" — the posterior third of the midbrain, formed by the colliculi.
Tegmentum
Latin "covering" — the middle midbrain region containing the reticular formation, many cranial nerve nuclei, and ascending/descending tracts.
Basis (pontis / pedunculi)
The most anterior region of the pons or midbrain, containing descending corticofugal fibers.
Crus cerebri
"Leg of the brain" — the paired ventral midbrain columns of descending corticospinal/corticonuclear/corticopontine fibers; also called basis pedunculi cerebri.
Peduncle
"Little foot/stalk" — a fiber bundle connecting two structures, e.g., the cerebellar peduncles.
Genu
"Knee" — a sharp bend in a fiber tract, e.g., the internal genu of CN VII around the abducens nucleus.
Ambiguus
"Uncertain/ambiguous" — the nucleus ambiguus, historically difficult to delineate precisely; motor nucleus for CN IX and X.
Solitarius (solitary)
"Alone" — the nucleus solitarius (solitary tract nucleus), a distinctive visceral/taste relay for CN VII, IX, and X.
Lemniscus
"Ribbon/band" — a flattened bundle of fibers, e.g., medial lemniscus, spinal (lateral) lemniscus.
Fasciculus
"Small bundle" — e.g., the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF).
Raphe
"Seam" — the midline nuclei of the brainstem, largely serotonergic.
Locus coeruleus
"Blue spot" — a pigmented nucleus and the main noradrenergic (norepinephrine) source for the brain.
Area postrema
"Area behind" — a circumventricular organ at the caudal fourth ventricle floor; the vomiting/chemoreceptor trigger zone.
Gracilis / Cuneatus
"Slender" / "wedge-shaped" — the dorsal column nuclei relaying lower-limb (gracilis) and upper-limb (cuneatus) proprioceptive/fine touch information.
Substantia nigra
"Black substance" — the pigmented, dopaminergic nucleus at the junction of the midbrain basis and tegmentum.
Cerebellopontine angle (CPA)
The recess between the cerebellum and pons where CN VII and VIII exit; a common tumor site (vestibular schwannoma).
Lissauer's tract
The dorsolateral fasciculus carrying first-order pain/temperature fibers before they synapse in the dorsal horn.
